'''James Edward Baggott''' (born 2 March 1957) is a British author living in [[Reading, Berkshire]], England who writes about science, philosophy, and science history. Baggott is the author of several books translated in many languages.

==Early life and education==

Baggott told science writer [[Brian Clegg (writer)|Brian Clegg]] that the reason why he went into the sciences was because he had some great schoolteachers. He loved physics but did not think he had a strong enough talent for the mathematics that would be required. "That said, my desire to seek explanations for things led me to [[chemical physics]] and it was with a great sense of pride and pleasure that I did manage to publish some entirely theoretical research papers, full of mathematical equations!"<ref name=Clegg>{{cite web|last1=Clegg|first1=Brian|authorlink=Brian Clegg (writer)|title=Jim Baggott – Four Way Interview|url=http://popsciencebooks.blogspot.co.uk/2012/09/jim-baggott-four-way-interview.html|website=Popular Science|accessdate=25 August 2015}}</ref>

He obtained his degree at the [[University of Manchester]] in 1978<ref name="Kaku">{{cite web |last=Kaku |first=Michio |authorlink=Michio Kaku |title=Science Fantastic: Michio talks Jim Baggott about the Plausibility of a 'Theory of Everything' |url=http://www.trn1.com/professor-michio-kaku-talks-with-jim-baggott-about-the-plausibility-of-a-_t |website=Science Fantastic |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304102020/http://www.trn1.com/professor-michio-kaku-talks-with-jim-baggott-about-the-plausibility-of-a-_t |archive-date=4 March 2016 |publisher=Talk Radio Network}}</ref>{{Time needed|date=May 2020}} and his DPhil in chemical physics at the [[University of Oxford]]. He worked as a professor for the [[University of Reading]] and left academia to work for [[Royal Dutch Shell|Shell International Petroleum]]. After several years he opened his own training and consultancy business. He calls himself a "science communicator" and publishes a science book approximately every 18 months.<ref name=Skepticality>{{cite web|last1=Colanduno|first1=Derek|authorlink= Derek Colanduno|title=Hello Reality|url=http://www.skepticality.com/hello-reality/|website=Skepticality|accessdate=22 August 2015}}</ref>

==''Higgs: The Invention and Discovery of the 'God Particle'''==

Baggott felt that scientists from [[CERN]] were getting close to discovering the [[Higgs boson]] and approached his editor about writing on the topic. His idea was to start writing the book, get about 95% done, and then, when the discovery was announced, he would be able to finish the last 5% and the book would be on the shelves very soon after the announcement.<ref name=Skepticality/> Throughout 2011 and 2012 he kept updating the book, leaving the last 1,500 words unsaid. He watched CERN's live webcast announce the discovery of the boson on 4 July and finished writing the book the next day.<ref name=Clegg/>

==''Farewell to Reality: How Modern Physics Has Betrayed the Search for Scientific Truth''==

Baggott got the idea to write ''Farewell to Reality: How Modern Physics Has Betrayed the Search for Scientific Truth'' and become a science activist when watching the [[BBC]] program ''What is Reality''. In his opinion, the program started out well, but became what he calls "fairy tale physics" when it included interviews with theoretical physicists who talked about such ideas as [[multiverse]], [[superstring theory]], and [[supersymmetry]]. These topics, according to Baggott, are fascinating to read about and are an entertaining way to make documentaries, sell books, or spend time at parties, but are "abstracted, theoretical speculation without any kind of empirical foundation" and "not science". ''Farewell to Reality'' is Baggott's attempt to counteract the "fuzzy science theory" and advocate for evidence and facts. Baggott states, "When you start asking 'Do we live in a hologram?' Then you are crossing into [[metaphysics]], and you are heading down the path of allowing all kinds of things that have no evidence to back it up, like [[creationism]]."<ref name=Skepticality/>

In an interview with [[Massimo Pigliucci]] on the ''Rationally Thinking'' podcast, Baggott stated that science is a human endeavour with a "fuzziness around the edges". He went on to say that there are no rules and, when training to be a scientist, no one gives you an instruction book on how to do science. "We kinda make it up as we go along... and it is perfectly reasonable for the scientific community to want to change those rules."<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pigliucci|first1=Massimo|authorlink=Massimo Pigliucci|title=RS116 – Jim Baggott and Massimo on Farewell to Reality|url=http://rationallyspeakingpodcast.org/show/rs116-jim-baggott-and-massimo-on-farewell-to-reality.html|website=Rationally Speaking|accessdate=24 August 2015|archive-date=1 June 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150601060043/http://rationallyspeakingpodcast.org/show/rs116-jim-baggott-and-massimo-on-farewell-to-reality.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Science writer [[Philip Ball]], in a review of ''Farewell'' in ''[[The Guardian]]'', stated that Baggott was right "although his target is as much the way this science is marketed as what it contains." Ball cautioned Baggott about criticising scientists who speculate because "conjecture injects vitality into science."<ref>{{cite web|last1=Ball|first1=Philip|authorlink=Philip Ball|title=Time Reborn by Lee Smolin; Farewell to Reality by Jim Baggott – review|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2013/jun/10/time-reborn-farewell-reality-review|work=The Guardian|accessdate=25 August 2015}}</ref>

Baggott, along with [[Jon Butterworth]], [[Hilary Rose (sociologist)|Hilary Rose]] and Stephen Minger, discussed the idea of futurist science theories with [[BBC Radio 4]] interviewer [[Allan Little]]. They discussed the likelihood that string theory and other theories that have yet to show empirical data will eventually be proved. Baggott expressed concern that "a body of professional theorists want to change the definition of what it means to do science". He feels that empirical data provides an anchor for these people to "return to reality" and that science without evidence is "most dangerous".<ref>{{cite web|last1=Little|first1=Allan|authorlink=Allan Little|title=Fairy Tale Physics?|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b0211hn3|website=BBC Radio 4|accessdate=27 August 2015}}</ref>

==''Beyond Measure''==
[[File:Jim Baggott-Crossing the Line-TAM 13 7-17-15.JPG|thumbnail|Jim Baggott addressing "Crossing the Line: The Challenge of Post-Empirical Science" at The Amaz!ng Meeting 13 (TAM 13), Friday 17 July 2015 at Tropicana, Las Vegas, Nevada.]]
Science writer [[Tony Hey]] writes that ''Beyond Measure'' was written for graduate and undergraduate physics students as an overview of quantum mechanics. The book has wider appeal by keeping the equations to the appendices for optional review. The book is divided into five parts starting with the history behind quantum theory, followed by the more recent experiments.  "Chapters on consciousness and on the ever-popular many-worlds interpretation of quantum theory form the conclusion."<ref name="Hey">{{cite news |last1=Hey |first1=Tony |title=A cat entangled in many worlds |url=https://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/books/a-cat-entangled-in-many-worlds/191259.article |work=Times Higher Education |date=17 September 2004 |accessdate=25 August 2015 |url-access=registration}}</ref>

|quote = <br />I don't advocate any kind of major change of direction. I just want us all to acknowledge the difference between empirically based scientific theories and metaphysics, or pseudo-science. I would question whether we should be throwing all our eggs in the string theory/multiverse/cosmic landscape basket. Perhaps it's time to consider other ways we might address the problems with the "authorized version" of reality, wherein all the available observational and experimental data are essentially secondary to the prevailing theoretical structures. These other ways would suffer from a lack of empirical foundations just the way string theory does, but there's a saying that when you find yourself in a deep hole, maybe it's time to stop digging..

==Publications==
Baggott is a regular contributor to ''[[New Scientist]]''<ref>{{cite web|title=New Scientist Search Jim Baggott|url=https://www.newscientist.com/search/?s=Jim+Baggott|work=New Scientist|accessdate=25 August 2015}}</ref>{{Third-party inline|date=May 2020}} and ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Jim Baggott|url=http://www.nature.com/search?journal=nature%2Cnews&q=jim%20baggott|website=Nature|accessdate=25 August 2015}}</ref>{{Third-party inline|date=May 2020}}
